synthesis.description: The real-time desk keeps each day's power schedules, imports and exports matched to the booked deals and to what the ISO and counterparties show. A round starts when the desk lead or a scheduler finds the desk long or short in a zone, a wrong schedule or import ID, a derated or cut path, or a counterparty limit. The email says what to buy or sell and for which book, which Enpower deals to enter, reprice or zero out, which tags and inc-sheet entries to complete, and whom to call, such as the CAISO, El Paso Electric or the preschedulers.
steps: The desk lead or a scheduler spots a long or short position, a wrong import or export, or a transmission derate or cut.
The position is checked against the schedule sheets, the Enpower deal entries and the ISO's records such as CAPS.
Traders buy or sell to fill the position, or arrange lending with El Paso Electric, for the book and price the email names.
Deals are entered, repriced or zeroed out in Enpower and deal scheduling, including cut schedules and the value of cut deals.
Tags and tag numbers go into the inc sheet and the EPE schedule sheet, tagged for both light and heavy load.
The desk calls the CAISO or the counterparty to confirm or change the schedule and summarises each deal in Pacific time.
Revenue from corrected deals is routed to the group that captures it, such as volume management.
The previous day's printed dispatch and prescheduling sheet are filed in the agreed folder for follow-up.

stalls.summary: The CAISO's systems fail during checkout: its computers go down and it again has difficulty reading the desk's bids, so schedules wait or have to be confirmed another way.

Schedule sheets carry errors that send rounds back for correction: a duplicate schedule in a sheet prepared ahead of the weekend, a wrong SPS volume, a wrong import ID, a period missing from the inc sheet, and an EPE schedule sheet that for yet another day leaves out schedules.

Deal entries are corrected after the fact: an El Paso Electric deal price is changed, a deal is zeroed out for part of the day, and a new deal summary shows revenue its writer says he should not receive.
Records that are lost or out of step have to be rebuilt: staff on shift must coordinate which deals were done and reconstruct a sheet, and a mismatch has to be squared away with the preschedulers.
Cut deals stay in the systems: the instruction to zero out cut deals in Enpower and value them is repeated later in capitals for deal scheduling.

The same procedures are restated in reminders, such as putting the tag number in the inc sheet, tagging both light and heavy load including the Southwest, and stating the Pacific time zone in deal summaries, which suggests these steps are often missed.
Short positions can be hard to fill: the desk reports asking every counterparty in the Northwest to sell it energy.
Follow-up work is put off to the next day when the desk lead has no time for it.

contradictions.summary: For the same schedule the desk expected a non-firm export, while CAPS showed a final firm import of the same size.

Volumes in the schedule records disagree with what was agreed: the SPS schedule shows a larger figure than it should for a delivery period, and an import ID carries the wrong on-peak and off-peak volumes.

After a deal price was changed, the new deal summary credits its writer with revenue he says he should not receive, while elsewhere revenue from a CAISO sale is said to go to the volume management group with no access for the real-time desk.

Different people are named for El Paso Electric schedule details: Kate as the source of prices and deal numbers for EPE lending, later Diane Cutsforth as working on the EPE schedule, while the previous day's EPE sheets still go to Kate Symes' old desk.

automation.approach: A checkout report could compare Enpower deal entries, the inc and EPE schedule sheets, the tags and the ISO's final schedules for each delivery period, flagging long or short positions, wrong import IDs or volumes, missing tag numbers and cut schedules not yet zeroed out. Traders would still decide what to buy or sell, call the ISO and counterparties, and value cut deals. A shift checklist would carry the recurring rules the desk lead keeps restating.
automation.rationale: The mail repeats the same reminders (tag numbers in the inc sheet, light and heavy load tags, Pacific time in deal summaries, zeroing out cut deals, filing the previous day's sheets) and shows errors that a routine check would catch before the ISO or a scheduler does. A shift checklist can be used straight away; the reconciliation report removes the manual comparison over time.

A simple extension takes about 10 minutes; a typical gap with a new ticket and re-allocation about 25; old strangers-gas cleanups and re-pathing up to 60. The search and matching are the automatable part; the deal decision and entry stay with people.

synthesis.description: Volume management and logistics staff find gas recorded at a meter with no valid deal or transport contract: a ticket has expired, flow began before a deal did, or old volumes sit in strangers gas. They ask the trader or desk for a spot, desk-to-desk or extended deal, or for approval to write the volume off to unaccounted-for gas. The trader creates or extends the ticket in Sitara and replies with the deal number; volume management applies, re-paths or brokers the volumes and sends the ticket back when its dates, price or counterparty are wrong.
steps: Volume management spots flow at a meter with no deal, an expired ticket or no contract while allocating volumes.
They check Sitara for the last deal ticket at the meter, its term and the contract tied to it.
They email the trader or desk with the meter, dates and volume, asking for a new or extended deal or a write-off approval.
The trader decides how the economics are handled and creates or extends the ticket, replying with the deal number.
Volume management checks the ticket's dates, price and counterparty and asks for a correction when it is wrong.
The volumes are applied, re-pathed or written off to unaccounted-for gas and the meter is cleared.

stalls.summary: Requests for a deal sit unanswered and have to be chased, leaving the flow unallocated until the trader replies.
Deals come back entered wrongly, with the wrong months or a price formula that has to be corrected, so the request goes round again.
Systems block the fix: a deal will not come across to Unify, a deal with an inactive or suspended counterparty cannot be extended, and flow does not carry over to mops.
Small volumes from flow recorded long before are left in strangers gas until logistics asks for a deal or for approval to write them off, so these problems stay open for a long time.

Requests reach the wrong person or miss people: an enquiry is first sent to someone who used to handle the work and then redirected, and a requester apologises for leaving a colleague off an earlier message.

contradictions.summary: The mail names different people as the one who sets up these deals: a counterparty and a sender citing Fred Boas point to Daren Farmer, while the same sender later says Danny Conner handles it.
A trader's pricing instruction for a new spot ticket was replaced by a different price formula in a follow-up, so the ticket had two conflicting instructions.
A deal cited to cover flow between ENA and HPL is contradicted by the reply that it is not a deal between those companies.

automation.approach: A daily exception report matching measured flow by meter against active deal tickets and transport contracts would list meters with flow and no valid deal, tickets nearing their end date, and counterparties that are inactive. Each exception would feed a standard request carrying the meter, dates, volume, last deal and contract to the trader, and small old volumes could be routed by rule to a write-off approval list.
automation.rationale: Most rounds start with a free-form note restating the same facts, and many come back wrong or unanswered. A standard request with the meter, dates, volume, counterparty, price basis and prior ticket gives traders what they need to enter the deal right the first time, and the report removes the manual search, while traders still decide the economics and enter the deals.

estimated.rationale: A round goes to research rather than email: finding the deal in Sitara, back-tracking to purchase invoices and confirmation sheets, comparing prices day by day, correcting the deal, and for power settlements going through ISO charges, schedules and service sheets. A single price check takes about 20 minutes; a typical discrepancy with research and correction about 45; multi-month or ISO reconciliations reach 120. Matching and variance flagging could be tool-driven; deciding disputes stays with people.

synthesis.description: A round starts when an invoice, payment, statement or ISO charge does not match what is booked: a counterparty bills a different price, a payment arrives that nobody can explain, a deal cannot be found in Sitara, or a capacity payment or congestion award looks wrong. Analysts search Sitara, back-track to purchase invoices and confirmation sheets, ask traders to verify pricing, correct deals, and decide whether to pay, hold or dispute the charge. Disputes are not to be raised with customers by email.
steps: An invoice, statement, payment or ISO settlement arrives that differs from the deal as booked.
The analyst looks up the deal in Sitara and compares price, volume and days with the confirmation and purchase invoices.
The trader or scheduler is asked to verify the price or explain the deal, such as a washout or a purchase to reverse.
The deal is corrected in Sitara, or the counterparty is asked to rebill at the confirmed price.
For power, ISO and PMA charges, capacity payments and congestion awards are checked against bids and schedules.
Unsupported charges are held from payment or disputed, and corrected billing is sent on.

stalls.summary: Analysts wait on traders, schedulers and counterparties to confirm prices or change the system, and send follow-ups asking whether anything was found.
Nobody is sure who handles a deal, an invoice or a billing, so items are forwarded to whoever might know, and an absence goes unnoticed while an item waits.
Sitara is not updated or holds conflicting prices, and no deal can be found for an invoiced amount, so the system has to be researched and corrected before settlement.
Information arrives late from the Hub, and ISO published prices do not match the bids, so charges cannot be settled until they are checked.

Old items resurface: an invoice for gas from months earlier that was never paid, purchase deals from a prior year still under research, and last year's incentive and service sheets to be gone through.

contradictions.summary: Counterparty invoices and confirmation sheets carry prices that differ from the deals as booked, and one counterparty changes its price again in the middle of the discussion.
Sitara holds two different prices for the same day on one deal.
Counterparty records disagree with the booked position: a counterparty's accountant does not show deals that are booked, and another counterparty cannot say why it received a payment.
ISO prices published for a congestion schedule do not match the bids submitted, and a capacity payment is questioned against the minimum rate expected for each hour.

automation.approach: An automated match of incoming invoices, statements and ISO settlement lines against Sitara deals could flag each price, volume or day mismatch with the confirmation alongside, and route the exception to the deal's owner from a maintained owner list. Analysts would then work only the flagged differences, with a standard discrepancy request carrying the deal number, days, invoiced price and booked price.
automation.rationale: Most rounds repeat the same lookups and comparisons, and the commonest stalls are waiting on replies and not knowing who owns a deal. A written procedure naming owners by counterparty and meter, the order of checks, when to hold payment, and that disputes are not emailed to customers addresses those directly, while the matching report removes the manual search.

estimated.rationale: Minutes go to reading the nomination form, checking it against the contract and transport, entering or changing volumes in Sitara and confirming with the pipeline. A routine daily nom sits near the low end of 10 minutes; revised or retroactive changes that need contract review, correction of earlier entries and rebalancing push toward 60 minutes. Mid 20 minutes reflects the mix of routine noms and revisions.

synthesis.description: Customers and suppliers such as Calpine, Enron Methanol and TXU send daily or monthly gas nominations, often as attached forms or spreadsheets. Schedulers enter the volumes in Sitara, set them up on the right contract and pipeline, and confirm. Revised nominations follow whenever volumes change, including retroactive changes that are checked against the contracts and corrected; traders and plant contacts forward changes such as plant swings or buybacks to be renominated, and the gas is then tracked and balanced.
steps: A customer or supplier sends a daily or monthly nomination, often as an attached form or spreadsheet.
The scheduler checks the request against the contract and the transport arrangements.
Estimated or nominated volumes are entered in Sitara on the right contract and meter.
The nomination is placed with the pipeline and confirmed back to the requester.
When volumes change, a revised nomination arrives and is forwarded to the scheduler responsible.
The scheduler updates the volumes, including retroactive corrections, and settles how any buyback is priced.
The gas is tracked and balanced against the nominated volumes.

stalls.summary: Schedulers wait on counterparties and colleagues: a supplier is still waiting on a transport number, a request goes unanswered until a follow-up asks whether it was checked, and an update waits on a returned phone call.

Volumes are changed repeatedly: a customer drops the volume again, another asks for a nomination to show zero, a supplier revises its nom for a span of days, and a scheduler corrects noms entered wrongly at the start of the month.
Customers request nomination changes retroactive to earlier dates, and management warns that retroactive deals affect daily operations and that contracts must be reviewed and understood.
An attachment with the full month position keeps bouncing off the mail gateway, so the position is pasted into the message body instead.
Nomination work is spread across several people, prompting a suggestion to centralize transport nominations and a later assignment of off-system nominations to one scheduler.

contradictions.summary: Volumes on the books disagree with what counterparties want: a customer is looking for a different February volume at a meter than nominated, another asks for a nomination to show zero instead, and a scheduler finds the noms entered at the start of the month were a mistake.

automation.approach: Standard nomination intake: counterparties submit a fixed spreadsheet layout that a tool reads into Sitara, compares with the previous nomination and the contract, and flags changed volumes, retroactive dates and missing transport numbers for the scheduler before the confirmation goes out. A shared list of nomination owners by pipeline routes each change to one person.
automation.rationale: Nominations arrive as Word forms, spreadsheets and pasted text, and much of the hands-on work is re-keying and comparing volumes. One nomination template that every counterparty fills in makes entry and comparison mechanical, leaving schedulers the judgement on retroactive changes, pricing and contract fit.

Most rounds cover a few days or one meter, so about 30 minutes is typical; a quick check is around 10, and a multi-month statement reconciliation or write-off review can reach 90. Pulling and comparing suit a report; investigation, calls and approvals stay with people.

synthesis.description: Schedulers, volume management and logistics staff compare what was scheduled or nominated with what was measured or actualized at meters and interconnects, often against a counterparty's or pipeline's own numbers (PG&E, HL&P, Transco, CIG, Mojave OBA). A round starts when someone spots a short day, a deal missing volume or a meter variance; the days or deals go to the other side, who verify pathing or send statements, and volumes are repathed, booked on tickets, absorbed by an OBA or written off to unaccounted-for gas with approval.
steps: A discrepancy surfaces: a short delivery day, a deal missing volume, or a meter where actualized flow differs from what was scheduled.
The scheduler lists the affected days, deals or meters and sends them to the counterparty, pipeline or internal owner to verify.
The other side checks pathing, nominations and measurement and returns volumes, production data or statements supporting the difference.
Volumes are moved or repathed, deals corrected, or tickets created to book the physical and economic impact.
Residual differences are absorbed by an OBA or, with logistics approval, written off to unaccounted-for gas.
An updated month-to-date flow or imbalance spreadsheet is circulated to traders and managers.

stalls.summary: Rounds wait on answers from colleagues and counterparties: voice mails go unanswered, a requester keeps asking when something will be ready, data for earlier months has to be retrieved by someone else, and one thread ends in a demand for an answer as soon as possible.

Requests bounce between people who are unsure who should answer: a request is passed on because it came from Settlements, a contact redirects the caller to someone else, and a person helps with a point that another person allocates.
Small-volume differences go round in circles, with staff asking whether an existing OBA could absorb them instead of reworking them each time.
A requested fix was told it was not a priority item, leaving the discrepancy open while the requester pressed for an urgent answer.
An erroneous recorded flow was not passed on to the measurement group, so the correction had to be chased later.

Some imbalances are left alone and grow: one item sits with a person because nobody wants to touch it, and staff note the cumulative imbalance is getting worse and ask for imbalances to be watched closely.

contradictions.summary: Mary Poorman writes that an imbalance item sits with her because nobody wants to touch it, then states that the daily imbalance check has been Bill's since the reorg, so the mail names two different holders of imbalance work.

On a meter discrepancy, Charlotte Hawkins apologises that Daren had to look into what he considers her responsibility, while saying the meter is pathed by Kim and only confirmed by her; elsewhere a manager assigns resolution with Transco to Charlotte.

automation.approach: A daily exception report that pulls scheduled, nominated and actualized volumes by meter, deal and day, compares them with counterparty statements, flags variances and cumulative imbalances beyond a set tolerance, and routes each to the named owner of that point; a standing month-to-date flow sheet fed from the same data replaces the hand-built spreadsheet.
automation.rationale: The comparison itself is data work a report can do, but the mail shows rounds stalling on who owns a point, who answers Settlements requests and who approves write-offs. A written procedure naming the owner for allocation, pathing, confirmation and write-off approval, with the order of checks, would cut the handoffs and repeated go-rounds first.

Single-deal flips are short; bankruptcy rounds with attached lists of many deals and a reconciliation take far longer, hence the wide range.

synthesis.description: Risk, settlements and desk staff move deals from one risk book to another. Early rounds flip single deals or a whole book's contents into the right regional or desk book, such as FT-US/CAND-ERMS, often by a stated deadline. After the bankruptcy filing, rounds move auto-terminating deals and terminated counterparties' deals into bankruptcy books from attached lists, followed by lists of stragglers. The receiver moves the deals in TAGG, zeroes them in Sitara, recalculates and officializes the book, and cross-references the result with other groups' lists.
steps: A requester identifies deals to move: single deals in the wrong book, a whole book's contents, or terminated counterparties' deals.
The deal list is compiled or forwarded, often as an attachment, naming the source and target book and a deadline.
The book owner moves each deal to the target book in the risk system, zeroing bankruptcy deals forward in Sitara.
The book is recalculated and officialized after the move.
The moved deals are cross-referenced against the requester's final list and other groups' calcs.
Stragglers found later are sent and moved in a follow-up round, and wrongly moved deals are moved back.

stalls.summary: Cross-checks wait on others: risk was still waiting on a final list to cross-reference with its calcs while settlements kept sending the deal lists behind terminated contracts.
Reconciling a book with another party's records needed help and the exact deal terms, and ended with the approach being redone a simpler way.
Bulk moves are rarely complete in one pass: one more deal, more deals and repeated batches of stragglers follow the first list.
Some moves are reversed: transactions already moved to the bankruptcy book had to be moved back to the live side.
Moves carry tight deadlines and repeated reminders, such as by the end of today, as soon as possible and right away.

contradictions.summary: Who leads the termination and bankruptcy-book work is named differently: one note says Darron and the writer will handle terminations from now on after Scott moved to another project, while a later note says Greg Couch will lead the estate risk effort.

Instructions on target books change mid-stream: deals are first moved from NG-Price to the bankruptcy book, then a later note changes the book used for terminated deals and renames NG-Price, and some deals moved into the bankruptcy book are sent back to the live side.

automation.approach: A standard deal-transfer request layout listing deal number, counterparty, current book, target book, effective date and reason, plus a risk-system query that pulls every deal for a terminated counterparty and flags those not yet in a bankruptcy book, so stragglers surface in one pass. After the move, a check compares the book's deals and totals with the request list before the book is officialized.
automation.rationale: Rounds repeat the same move with lists that arrive in pieces and in varying formats, and keep producing stragglers and reversals. One request template with fixed columns lets the book owner move and check deals line by line, and is the input a query or bulk-move script would read; deciding which deals belong in which book stays with risk staff.

The report holds a handful of figures in a fixed form, so about 20 minutes is typical, 10 in a quiet week with no bullets, and up to 40 when line pack sales or an outside report are added. The figure work suits automation; the bullets remain manual.

synthesis.description: Each week the Transwestern commercial team sends a California Capacity Report giving the pipeline's average deliveries to California, their share of capacity and San Juan lateral throughput, sometimes with operational line pack sold and its average rate, alongside a short bullet summary of ongoing deals. One person compiles it and sends it to the team and managers; outside reports such as the CEC draft are passed along on request, and a misdated report is corrected by a follow-up.
steps: Pull the week's daily delivery volumes to California and the San Juan lateral throughput.
Compute average daily deliveries and their share of capacity.
Add any operational line pack sold during the week and its average rate.
Collect the weekly bullets on ongoing deals, or note that there are none.
Send the California Capacity Report for the week's dates to the commercial team and managers.
Resend with a correction when the report's dates were wrong.

automation.rationale: The report repeats the same sentences with new figures every week, so a fixed layout fed by the data removes the recalculation and the misdated-week errors; the bullet summary of deals still needs the commercial lead's judgement.

Posting generation, validation and notices can be tooled; approvals and disputes cannot.

synthesis.description: Marketing Transwestern's available firm capacity and handling capacity changes. A round starts with a draft capacity posting, a shipper or internal request to raise a contract's daily quantity, or a push to market capacity to a new customer such as a power plant. The commercial lead has colleagues review the posting, puts it on the EBB, forwards the link to shippers with the bid deadline that afternoon, approves quantity increases, checks contract notice clauses, and reports posting errors and late postings.
steps: The commercial lead drafts a posting of available firm capacity or receives a request to change a contract quantity.
Colleagues review the draft posting before it goes up.
The posting goes live on the EBB and the link is forwarded to shippers with the bid deadline.
Bid-day reminders go out again to prospective bidders.
Requests to raise a daily quantity are approved and passed on so the contract quantity is changed in the system.
Contract clauses such as notice before expiration are checked when capacity is returned or released.
Posting errors and late postings are reported and fixed.

stalls.summary: Postings fail or slip: the unsubscribed capacity form on the EBB threw an error, and a posting went up late again.

A standard handover checklist with owners and deadlines answers the recurring questions about which files and procedures stay with the estate and keeps requests from reaching the wrong person, while decisions such as a liquidation plan stay with people.

Requests wait on people: an assigned analysis has made little progress, and a question is held until a colleague returns the next day.

automation.rationale: Rounds stall mostly on not knowing who owns a deal and on requests that lack the detail needed to act. A fixed request layout with an owner lookup by desk sends each correction to the right person with everything needed to make the change, while the edits themselves still need a person with rights to the deal.

automation.rationale: Rounds repeat the same steps but stall on cancelled interviews, late feedback, approvals and unclear HR routing; a checklist makes each hand-off and its owner explicit. Outage timing arrives second-hand and changes: an interconnect's downtime is passed on as what the sender is being told, and a scheduled outage turns out to be postponed, so plans built on the first notice have to be redone.

automation.approach: A shared outage log fed by a standard notice: each entry records the meter or point, pipeline, start and expected end, volume before and after, and cause. A lookup from meter to the deals and counterparties flowing there lists who is affected, drafts the customer notices and flags nominations to change; restart updates amend the same entry instead of starting a new thread.
automation.rationale: Notices come from many senders in free text, and some leave out the meter, the volumes or the end date, which forces follow-up calls. A standard outage notice that always carries those fields lets schedulers find affected deals quickly and is the first step toward the log and lookup. Deciding how to replace supply and whether force majeure applies stays with people.

A request names the meter, the production months and the contract the volumes should go to.
The allocation set-up is changed: contract, ranking, percentages or volume overrides.
Allocation statements are reviewed and corrections agreed with the responsible scheduler.

automation.approach: An exception report comparing each meter's allocated volumes with its contract, ranking and percentage set-up, flagging meters that fail to allocate or land on the wrong contract, paired with a standard change request form naming the meter, months, target contract, ranking or percentage, requester and the owner in volume management who makes the change.
automation.rationale: The stalls come from requests understood differently, unclear owners and changes waiting on others. A request form with fixed fields and a named owner removes most of the handoff confusion, and the exception report finds faults before counterparts do; deciding which contract is right stays with people.

automation.rationale: The stalls come from incomplete pathing, unclear routing of requests and setups challenged after the fact. A complete request form and an unpathed-deal report catch these before the requester has to chase, while choosing paths and handling exceptions stay with schedulers.

automation.rationale: The round is a question-and-answer loop between validation and the desk, and the answers are short market explanations that recur. A standard curve-change explanation log removes the forward-and-wait step and gives the validation group one place to read the reasons.

Deciding who covers what and training the successor remain work for people.

synthesis.description: Employees file expense reports through Concur (one request names Enron's XMS system). Concur emails the approver that a report is ready for approval and later that its approval status has changed; the approver reviews the items and approves or rejects them. Assistants also ask colleagues for outstanding items to be expensed, and during the bankruptcy announcements push approvers to clear reports waiting in their inboxes and explain which bills fall under pre-petition.
steps: An employee or assistant gathers outstanding invoices and receipts to be expensed.
The expense report is filed in the Concur expense system.
Concur notifies the approver that the report is ready for approval.
The approver reviews the items and approves or rejects the report.
Concur notifies the submitter that the approval status has changed.
The expenses are reimbursed, with bills treated according to whether they were submitted before the pre-petition cutoff.

stalls.summary: A submitter cannot get into the expense system and asks for help with the Concur login and password, so the report waits until access is restored.

Reports sit unprocessed: an announcement asks approvers to either approve or reject the outstanding business expenses in their inboxes, and staff are asked to file the outstanding employee expenses they hold as soon as possible.

contradictions.summary: One announcement says expenses will be reimbursed promptly upon submission, while another sorts bills by whether they were submitted before a mid-December date and treats those as covered under pre-petition, so the treatment of an item depends on when it was submitted.

automation.approach: A daily report from the expense system listing reports awaiting approval by approver and age, with automatic reminders, plus rule checks that flag items missing receipts, outside policy, or on the wrong side of the pre-petition cutoff so approvers look closely only at flagged items. Self-service password reset would remove the login stall.
automation.rationale: The system already routes reports, so the remaining hands-on work is the approver's review and the submitter's gathering of invoices. A short checklist covering what to attach, the bankruptcy cutoff rules and how to regain system access would reduce rejected and stuck reports soonest; the queue report addresses reports left sitting in inboxes.

synthesis.description: A desk accountant reports the origination recognized in the nightly run, broken down by desk, and tells originators when their credit has or has not shown up. He traces individual originators' deals, codes all origination, including Denver's, to a single cost centre, and books corrections in a later month so the quarter's gas P&L is right. When an originator's group asks for data on its deals, he sets up a daily origination report for them.
steps: Run the nightly origination recognition and note the totals by desk.
Tell the originators and their groups what origination was recognized.
Compare recognized origination with the schedule and flag differences.
Trace missing originations for individual originators.
Code origination to the agreed cost centre.
Book corrections in a later month to fix the quarter's P&L.
Send deal data and a daily origination report to the groups that ask for them.

stalls.summary: Originations that do not appear where expected have to be traced by hand for a named originator.
Mistakes surface after the books close and are fixed with corrections in a later month to set the quarter's gas P&L right, which means rework.
Origination credit depends on someone else booking it, and the originator is told to wait for the entry to appear that night.

contradictions.summary: The two sides' figures disagree: one party has recognized an amount of origination that the desk accountant does not see on his side, so the two sets of records have to be reconciled.

automation.approach: Build a daily reconciliation report that compares origination recognized in the books with the origination schedule by originator, desk and cost centre. It would flag missing, mismatched or miscoded entries before close, and the same output would go to the groups that want a daily origination report.
automation.rationale: The quotes show a single accountant tracing missing originations, explaining mismatched figures and booking late corrections. A standard reconciliation layout makes differences visible every day instead of after the quarter's P&L is affected, and it is also the report the groups ask for.

synthesis.description: Gas sales and purchases are confirmed in writing with counterparties and internal groups. A round starts when the desk sends a copy of a confirmation or a notice of a sale, such as the pipeline selling operational gas to Western from April, or when a counterparty asks for a Transaction Confirmation sheet for a volume at a delivery point, or reports that confirmations for several months never arrived. The deal terms are pulled from the deal record and sent, and the recipient checks them against its own records.
steps: A sale or purchase is agreed, or a counterparty asks for written confirmation of a deal.
The desk pulls the deal terms (volume, delivery point, period) from the deal record.
The confirmation sheet or notice is prepared and sent to the counterparty and the internal groups that need it.
The counterparty checks the confirmation against its own records.
When confirmations are missing, the counterparty raises it and the desk sends the outstanding ones.

stalls.summary: A counterparty's fuel buyer reports never receiving confirmations for May, June and July, so a run of confirmations went missing before anyone noticed.
When the pipeline sells operational gas to Western, the sender is unsure how the information reaches the group that needs it, so the routing of confirmations is unclear.

automation.approach: Generate the confirmation from the deal record when a deal is entered, send it to a standard distribution list per counterparty and internal group, and keep a log of confirmations sent and acknowledged so a report flags any deal or month without a confirmation before the counterparty has to ask.
automation.rationale: The stalls are a run of confirmations that never arrived and uncertainty over who receives sale information. A standard confirmation form filled from the deal record, with a named distribution, addresses both, while people still review terms and handle disputes with the counterparty.

synthesis.description: Managers and staff ask HR or payroll to change employee records. Requests include moving employees to a different operating company, stopping payroll deductions such as United Way contributions from a stated date, adding staff missing from the HR system, arranging an exit interview, and clarifying a departing employee's separation entitlements. In a round, someone sends a request to HR, HR looks up or changes the record, and HR confirms back to the requester, who may pass the answer on to the employee.
steps: A manager or employee asks HR or payroll to change a record, a deduction or an entitlement.
HR looks up the employee in the HR system and checks what is recorded.
HR makes the change, adds the missing person, or works out the entitlement in question.
HR confirms the outcome to the requester.
The requester passes the answer on to the employee or arranges the next step, such as an exit interview.

stalls.summary: A manager answering a departing employee's request for clarification had to wait for HR and asked to be told as soon as there was an answer.
One new employee was in the system and another was not, so the missing record had to be set up before the request could go ahead.

automation.approach: A standard HR change request form that records the employee, the type of change (operating company, supervisor, deduction or separation), the date it takes effect and the approver. The form goes to the HR contact and shows the requester its status. Employees could stop deductions themselves, and a new-starter check could compare the HR system with the team roster to flag anyone missing.
automation.rationale: The rounds are short requests, slowed by missing details and by waiting for a reply. A form with the fields HR needs, and a status the requester can see, cuts the back-and-forth. Separation entitlements and exits still need HR's judgement.

synthesis.description: Employees ask their manager (Bill Williams) for particular days off or a longer vacation. The manager replies approving the dates, telling staff to take the days and to give notice of longer vacations in advance as everyone else in the group does. The approved days are put down on the group's vacation calendar, and staff ask to be put down for further dates as needed.
steps: Employee emails the manager asking for particular days off or a vacation.
Manager checks the dates against the group's coverage and other planned absences.
Manager replies approving the days, asking for advance notice of longer vacations.
The approved dates are entered on the vacation calendar, and further dates are added on request.

automation.approach: A shared leave calendar with a short request form: the employee enters the dates, the manager sees overlapping absences and approves in one step, and approved dates land on the calendar without being re-keyed.
automation.rationale: The work is small and repetitive: checking overlap and recording dates. A standard request and calendar layout keeps approvals and the calendar in step, while the coverage decision stays with the manager.
